mainTopic: The law of רודף and its Torah sources, and the duty to rescue someone in danger.
overview: The משנה lists pursuers who may be stopped even by killing them: someone chasing a person to kill him, someone chasing a male, and someone chasing a נערה המאורסה. Sinners with no human victim may not be stopped this way. The גמרא first tries 'לא תעמד על דם רעך' as the source, but agrees that this פסוק teaches the duty to rescue. It then tries a קל וחומר from נערה המאורסה, and replaces it with a הקש because אין עונשין מן הדין. The murder case 'comes to teach and ends up learning', and the נערה's own rule comes from 'ואין מושיע לה'. Next the גמרא explains that 'לא תעמד' adds a duty to go to trouble and even hire help, beyond what והשבתו לו teaches. A ברייתא then lists which forbidden relationships allow killing the pursuer, with limits on when he may be killed. All the cases are learned from the words נער, נערה, חטא and מות in one פסוק. The גמרא begins showing why each case is needed, and that discussion continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The משנה: which pursuers may be stopped even by killing them
steps.stepSummary: The משנה lists three pursuers who may be stopped at the cost of their lives. It also lists three sinners who may not be stopped that way.
steps.simpleTranslation: These people are stopped even if it costs their lives: someone chasing another person to kill him, someone chasing a male to violate him, and someone chasing a betrothed young woman to violate her. But someone chasing an animal, someone about to break שבת, and someone about to worship idols may not be stopped by killing them.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives a list of pursuers whom we may stop even by killing them, and a list of sinners whom we may not stop that way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first group, the sin harms another person: a life, or the dignity of a victim. In the second group, there is no human victim being hurt. Those sinners are warned and judged in בית דין later; they are not killed on the spot.

keyTerms.meaning: The משנה being studied
A pursuer, someone chasing another person to harm him
We save them (or the victim) at the cost of their lives, meaning the pursuer may be killed
A betrothed young girl
A male

steps.confusionAlert: 'מצילין אותן בנפשן' does not mean we save their lives. It means we stop them even if they die in the process. The idea is to stop them before they sin and to save the victim.
steps.whyThisMatters: This משנה is the main source for the הלכה of רודף: someone who is about to kill may be stopped with deadly force.

phrases.english: MISHNAH: And these are the ones
who are saved at the cost of their lives:
phrases.notes: This means we stop them from sinning, even if that means killing them.

phrases.english: one who chases after his fellow to kill him,
and after a male,
and after a betrothed young woman.
But one who chases after an animal,
and one who desecrates Shabbat,
and one who worships idols –
they are not saved at the cost of their lives.

steps.mimraCoreRuling: A pursuer who threatens a life, a male, or a נערה המאורסה may be stopped by killing him. Sinners with no human victim (animal, שבת, עבודה זרה) may not.

steps.title: A ברייתא gives a source: 'Do not stand by your fellow's blood'
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא learns that we may save the victim of a רודף, even at the cost of the רודף's life, from the פסוק 'לא תעמד על דם רעך'.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: How do we know that when someone chases another to kill him, the victim may be saved even at the cost of the pursuer's life? The פסוק says, 'Do not stand idly by your fellow's blood.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that gives a Torah source for the first case of the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא reads the פסוק as an order not to sit back while someone's blood is about to be spilled. So, it says, you may even kill the pursuer to save the victim.

keyTerms.meaning: The Rabbis taught; this opens a ברייתא
From where do we know?
He may be saved at the cost of the pursuer's life
The פסוק says

phrases.english: GEMARA: The Rabbis taught:
From where do we know, about one who chases his fellow to kill him,
that he may be saved at the cost of the pursuer's life?
phrases.notes: 'Him' is the victim; 'his life' is the pursuer's life.

phrases.english: The verse teaches:
"Do not stand by the blood of your fellow."

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: מִנַּיִין לְרוֹדֵף אַחַר חֲבֵירוֹ לְהׇרְגוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a source for the first case of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The source for saving a victim at the pursuer's expense is 'לא תעמד על דם רעך'.

steps.title: That verse is already needed for the duty to rescue
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects: 'לא תעמד על דם רעך' is already used by another ברייתא to teach that you must rescue someone in danger.
steps.simpleTranslation: But is that what this פסוק comes to teach? It is needed for another ברייתא: How do we know that if you see someone drowning in a river, or being dragged by a wild animal, or attacked by bandits, you must save him? The פסוק says, 'Do not stand idly by your fellow's blood.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא's source. It says the פסוק is already being used for something else.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The plain meaning of the פסוק is a duty to rescue a person in danger. That is a different law from being allowed to kill a pursuer. A פסוק that is needed for one law cannot simply be used for a second law too.

keyTerms.meaning: But does it really come for this?
It is needed for
As is taught in a ברייתא
Bandits

phrases.english: But does this come for this purpose?
This is needed for what was taught:
From where do we know, about one who sees his fellow
drowning in a river,
or a wild animal dragging him,
or bandits coming upon him,
that he is obligated to save him?

phrases.aramaic: תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר: ״לֹא תַעֲמֹד עַל דַּם רֵעֶךָ״.
phrases.english: The verse teaches: "Do not stand by the blood of your fellow."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the source given in step 2.
steps.kashyaTarget: The use of 'לא תעמד על דם רעך' as the source for killing a רודף.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק is already needed for the general duty to rescue, so it is not free to teach permission to kill the pursuer.

steps.title: The גמרא agrees
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא accepts the challenge: yes, the פסוק teaches the duty to rescue.
steps.simpleTranslation: Yes, that is indeed so.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא agrees that the פסוק is about the duty to save someone in danger. This sets up the next question: where, then, does permission to kill the pursuer come from?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of defending the ברייתא's source, the גמרא gives in on this point. The duty to rescue stays in the פסוק, but the permission to kill a רודף now needs a different source.

keyTerms.meaning: Yes, it is indeed so (a concession)

phrases.english: Yes, it is indeed so.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Agrees with the challenge of step 3.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוק itself permits killing the רודף.
steps.terutzMaskana: The פסוק teaches only the duty to rescue; the permission to kill needs another source.

steps.title: Then where do we learn that the pursuer may be killed?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for a new source for the permission to save the victim at the cost of the pursuer's life.
steps.simpleTranslation: But then, how do we know that the victim may be saved at the cost of the pursuer's life?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for a new source. This sets up the next answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The duty to rescue is already known. What is still missing is the permission to kill the pursuer, so the גמרא asks for a separate source for that.

keyTerms.meaning: From where do we know it?
But then

phrases.english: But then, that he may be saved at the cost of the pursuer's life, from where do we know it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows from the concession in step 4.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A source for the permission to kill a רודף.

steps.title: A קל וחומר from the נערה המאורסה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא learns the law with a קל וחומר: if a נערה המאורסה may be saved at the attacker's life, then surely someone whose life is in danger may be.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is learned by a קל וחומר from a betrothed young woman. The attacker of a נערה המאורסה only comes to harm her status, and still the Torah said she may be saved at the cost of his life. Someone chasing another to kill him, all the more so!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a קל וחומר from the case of the נערה המאורסה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah lets us kill the attacker of a נערה המאורסה, even though he 'only' damages her. A murderer takes a whole life, which is far worse. So the permission should surely apply to him.

keyTerms.meaning: A logical argument from a lighter case to a stricter one
It comes (is learned) from
To damage or degrade her
All the more so

phrases.english: It is learned by a kal vachomer from a betrothed young woman:
Just as a betrothed young woman,
whom he comes only to degrade,
the Torah said she may be saved at the cost of his life,
one who chases his fellow to kill him –
all the more so.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 5.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A קל וחומר from נערה המאורסה, where the Torah allows killing the attacker.

steps.title: We don't punish based on logic alone
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the קל וחומר: we do not punish someone based only on a קל וחומר.
steps.simpleTranslation: But do we punish based on a logical argument?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the קל וחומר. Killing the רודף is a kind of punishment, and there is a rule that we do not punish based on a קל וחומר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule 'אין עונשין מן הדין' says a punishment must be written in the Torah or learned in some way stronger than logic alone. So the קל וחומר is not enough to allow taking the pursuer's life.

keyTerms.meaning: Do we punish based on a קל וחומר? (No: אין עונשין מן הדין)

phrases.english: But do we punish based on a logical inference?
phrases.notes: Here 'הדין' means the קל וחומר just given.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the method used in step 6.
steps.kashyaTarget: The קל וחומר from נערה המאורסה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A punishment cannot be based only on a קל וחומר.

steps.title: The school of רבי: it is a הקש
steps.stepSummary: The school of רבי teaches that the law comes from a הקש, a פסוק that puts murder side by side with the attack on a נערה המאורסה.
steps.simpleTranslation: A teacher from the school of רבי taught: It is a הקש. The פסוק says, 'For just as a man rises against his fellow and murders him.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the source is not just logic. It is a הקש, a comparison that comes from the Torah itself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the passage about the נערה המאורסה, the Torah mentions a murderer. That puts the two cases side by side. Because the comparison is written in the Torah, it is strong enough to allow taking a life.

keyTerms.meaning: A teacher from the school of רבי taught
A הקש: a comparison learned from two topics placed together in a פסוק
And murders him

phrases.english: A teacher of the school of Rebbi taught:
It is a juxtaposition:
"For just as a man rises against his fellow
phrases.notes: דברים 22:26, in the passage about the נערה המאורסה.

phrases.english: and murders him."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 7.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Brings a stronger source (a הקש instead of a קל וחומר)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The law depends only on a קל וחומר, which cannot be used for punishment.
steps.terutzMaskana: A הקש in the Torah links murder with נערה המאורסה, so punishment may be learned from it.

steps.title: What do we learn from the murderer?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the mention of a murderer in the נערה המאורסה passage is meant to teach. This sets up the explanation of the הקש.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what have we learned from a murderer?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why the Torah mentions murder in this passage. It is setting up an explanation of how the הקש works, which comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before the comparison can be used, we must understand what point it is making. The next step answers this: the murder case both teaches about the נערה המאורסה and learns from her.

keyTerms.meaning: What have we learned?
A murderer

phrases.english: And what have we learned from a murderer?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts explaining the הקש brought in step 8.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What point the Torah is making by comparing the murderer to the attacker of a נערה המאורסה.

steps.title: The murder case teaches and also learns
steps.stepSummary: The murder case was put in the נערה המאורסה passage to teach something about her, but it also learns back from her: just as she may be saved at the attacker's life, so may a murder victim.
steps.simpleTranslation: Now the murder case came to teach, and it turns out it also learns. The פסוק compares a murderer to a נערה המאורסה: just as she may be saved at the cost of the attacker's life, so too a murder victim may be saved at the cost of the murderer's life.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 9. The murder case teaches about the נערה המאורסה, and it also learns the life-saving law back from her.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Usually a comparison runs one way. Here it runs both ways. The murder case was mentioned to teach about the נערה המאורסה, and the same הקש also lets it learn her rule: you may save the victim even by killing the attacker.

keyTerms.meaning: It came to teach, and it turns out it also learns
Compares (by placing two cases side by side in a פסוק)
One may save him at the cost of the attacker's life
Murderer (here, someone trying to murder)

steps.whatToRemember: The source for killing a רודף to save a murder victim is the הקש to נערה המאורסה.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the main source for the law of רודף: you may stop someone trying to murder, even by killing him.

phrases.english: Now, this came to teach
phrases.notes: 'This' is the mention of murder in the נערה המאורסה passage.

phrases.english: and it turns out that it learns.
It compares a murderer to a betrothed young woman:
just as with a betrothed young woman
one may save her at the cost of his life,
so too with a murderer
one may save him at the cost of his life.

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵעַתָּה הֲרֵי זֶה בָּא לְלַמֵּד וְנִמְצָא לָמֵד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 9's question about why the murderer is mentioned, and finishes explaining the הקש from step 8.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The murder case teaches about the נערה המאורסה and also learns from her that the victim may be saved at the attacker's life.

steps.title: Where do we learn the rule for the betrothed young woman herself?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the source that a נערה המאורסה may be saved at the attacker's life.
steps.simpleTranslation: And for the betrothed young woman herself, where do we learn this?
steps.whatsHappening: The murder case learns its rule from the נערה המאורסה. So the גמרא asks where her own rule comes from. This sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A הקש only works if the case we learn from has a clear source. The גמרא now checks that base.

keyTerms.meaning: Herself, the case itself
From where do we know?
A betrothed young woman (after קידושין, before נישואין)

phrases.english: And the betrothed young woman herself, from where do we derive it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of the base case that step 10 learned from.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source that a נערה המאורסה may be saved at the cost of the attacker's life.

steps.title: 'There was none to save her' means anyone who can must save her
steps.stepSummary: The school of רבי ישמעאל reads 'and there was none to save her' to mean that if someone is able to save her, he must do it by any means, even killing the attacker.
steps.simpleTranslation: As the school of רבי ישמעאל taught: 'and there was none to save her.' This means that if there is someone to save her, he saves her by any means that can save her.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the source for the נערה המאורסה: a ברייתא from the school of רבי ישמעאל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says she cried out 'and there was none to save her.' That implies that if someone is there, he must save her. 'By any means' includes killing the attacker.

keyTerms.meaning: The school (study house) of רבי ישמעאל
A rescuer, someone who saves
By any means that can save

phrases.english: As was taught in the school of Rabbi Yishmael,
for it was taught in the school of Rabbi Yishmael:
'And there was none to save her',
but if there is someone to save her,
he saves her by any means that can save her.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 11's question.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: From 'ואין מושיע לה': if a rescuer is there, he saves her by any means, even the attacker's life.
steps.whatToRemember: The chain is: נערה המאורסה (from 'ואין מושיע לה') leads to murder victim (by the הקש). In both cases the victim may be saved at the attacker's life.

steps.title: The duty to save someone drowning, attacked by an animal, or by bandits
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the ברייתא: someone who sees another in danger must save him, learned from 'לא תעמוד על דם רעך'.
steps.simpleTranslation: Back to the matter itself: from where do we know that someone who sees his friend drowning in a river, or being dragged by a wild animal, or attacked by bandits, must save him? The פסוק says: 'Do not stand idly by the blood of your fellow.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to look at a ברייתא it quoted earlier. It teaches that you must save someone in danger, based on לא תעמוד על דם רעך. This sets up the question in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before, the topic was whether you may kill an attacker. Now the topic is a duty: you are required to rescue. The source given is לא תעמוד על דם רעך.

keyTerms.meaning: The matter itself: going back to examine a source quoted earlier
Bandits, robbers
The פסוק teaches
Do not stand idly by the blood of your fellow

phrases.english: The matter itself: from where do we know that one who sees his fellow
phrases.notes: גופא means the גמרא is going back to study a ברייתא it quoted earlier, on its own.

phrases.english: drowning in a river,
or a wild animal dragging him,
or bandits coming upon him,
is obligated to save him?

phrases.aramaic: תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר: ״לֹא תַעֲמֹד עַל דַּם רֵעֶךָ״.
phrases.english: The verse states: 'Do not stand idly by the blood of your fellow.'

steps.triggerLanguage: גּוּפָא: מִנַּיִן לָרוֹאֶה אֶת חֲבֵרוֹ שֶׁהוּא טוֹבֵעַ בַּנָּהָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the רודף topic and goes back to examine a ברייתא quoted earlier about the duty to rescue.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One who sees another in danger must save him, from לא תעמוד על דם רעך.

steps.title: Isn't the duty to rescue already learned from returning lost property?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: the duty to save a person's body is already learned from 'והשבתו לו', so why do we need לא תעמוד?
steps.simpleTranslation: But is this learned from here? It is learned from there! From where do we know about the loss of a person's body? The פסוק says: 'And you shall return it to him.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא in step 13. Another פסוק already seems to teach the duty to rescue.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק about returning a lost object, והשבתו לו, is also read as 'return him to himself,' meaning save his body. If that already teaches the duty to rescue, then לא תעמוד על דם רעך looks unnecessary.

keyTerms.meaning: From here / from there
It is derived, it comes out
The loss of his body (danger to his life or health)
And you shall return it to him

phrases.english: But is it derived from here?
It is derived from there!
From where do we know about the loss of his body?
The verse states: 'And you shall return it to him.'
phrases.notes: דברים 22:2. This פסוק is about a lost object, but here it's read as 'return him to himself,' meaning save his body.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the source given in step 13 as unnecessary.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's use of לא תעמוד על דם רעך as the source for the duty to rescue.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: והשבתו לו already teaches the duty to save a person's body, so a second פסוק should not be needed.

steps.title: לא תעמוד adds the duty to go to trouble and hire help
steps.stepSummary: From והשבתו לו alone we would think you only have to save him yourself. לא תעמוד teaches that you must also go to trouble and even hire people to save him.
steps.simpleTranslation: If we only had the source from there, I would have thought: that is only when he saves him personally. But to go to trouble and hire workers, I would say he does not have to. So the פסוק teaches us that he must.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge in step 14. Each פסוק teaches something different, so both are needed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: והשבתו לו is about returning a lost object, so it would only require you to act personally. לא תעמוד על דם רעך goes further: you must make an effort and even pay others to help save him.

keyTerms.meaning: I would have thought (before the answer)
To go to trouble, to make an effort
To hire workers
It teaches us (that the first idea is wrong)

steps.confusionAlert: Here בְּנַפְשֵׁיהּ means 'by himself, personally.' It does not mean 'at the cost of his life,' like בנפשו earlier in this סוגיא.
steps.whatToRemember: והשבתו לו teaches that you must save someone personally. לא תעמוד על דם רעך adds that you must go to trouble and even hire people to save him.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the halachic scope of the duty to rescue: it includes effort and spending money, not only acting yourself.

phrases.english: If it were only from there, I would have said:
this applies only by himself,
phrases.notes: He means saving him personally, with your own hands.

phrases.english: but to go to trouble and hire workers,
I would say no.
So it teaches us.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves step 14's challenge by showing that לא תעמוד teaches something extra.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Each of the two פסוקים teaches a different level of the duty.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: From והשבתו לו alone, one only has to save the person himself, not go to trouble or hire help.
steps.terutzMaskana: לא תעמוד על דם רעך requires going to trouble and even hiring workers to save him.

steps.title: Which pursuers may be stopped by killing them
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא lists the pursuers who may be killed to save the victim. It also lists the forbidden relationships where we may not kill the pursuer.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages taught: someone chasing another person to kill him, or chasing a male, a נערה המאורסה, or a woman forbidden to him under a court death penalty or כרת, may be stopped even by killing him. But if a כהן גדול chases a widow, or a regular כהן chases a divorcée or a חלוצה, we may not kill him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא. It lists the cases where we may save the victim even by killing the attacker, and the cases where we may not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Killing the pursuer is allowed only when the act he is chasing is very severe: murder, or a relationship punished by מיתת בית דין or כרת. A widow with a כהן גדול, or a divorcée or חלוצה with a regular כהן, is only a plain לאו. Those sins are not severe enough to allow killing the attacker.

keyTerms.meaning: A pursuer, someone chasing another person to harm him
We save them at the cost of his (the pursuer's) life
Relationships punished by כרת (being cut off)
Relationships punished by a death penalty given by בית דין
A woman who did חליצה and may not marry a כהן

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the widow, divorcée and חלוצה cases are allowed relationships. They are still forbidden. The point is only that they are not severe enough to allow killing the pursuer.

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
Whether one who chases after his fellow to kill him,
or after a male,
or after a betrothed young woman,
or after women for whom one is liable to a court death penalty,
or after women for whom one is liable to כרת,
they are saved at the cost of his life.
A widow chased by a High Priest,
a divorcée or a חלוצה chased by an ordinary priest,
they are not saved at the cost of his life.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: אֶחָד הָרוֹדֵף אַחַר חֲבֵירוֹ לְהׇרְגוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new ברייתא on the topic of a רודף, after the discussion of לא תעמוד על דם רעך.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Pursuers chasing to murder, to force relations with a male or a נערה המאורסה, or to commit a sin punished by מיתת בית דין or כרת may be stopped by killing them. Pursuers chasing to commit a sin that is only a לאו may not.

steps.title: When we may not kill the pursuer of a betrothed girl
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues. We do not kill the pursuer if the sin already happened, or if she can be saved another way. רבי יהודה adds the case where she says to leave him alone.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the sin was already done to her, we do not save her by killing him. If she has someone who can save her another way, we do not kill him. רבי יהודה says: even if she says 'leave him alone', so that he will not kill her, we do not kill him.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא now gives limits. These are cases where, even though the act is very severe, we still may not kill the pursuer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Killing a רודף is meant only to stop the sin. If the sin already happened, killing him no longer saves anything. If there is another way to save her, killing him is not needed. רבי יהודה adds that if she tells the rescuers to leave him, because she fears he will kill her, we also do not kill him.

keyTerms.meaning: The sin was already done with her
A rescuer, a way to save her without killing
Leave him alone

steps.whyThisMatters: These limits show that permission to kill a רודף exists only to prevent the harm. It is not a punishment.

phrases.english: If a sin was already done with her,
we do not save her at the cost of his life.
If she has someone to rescue her,
we do not save her at the cost of his life.
Rabbi Yehuda says:
Also one who says, "Leave him alone,"
so that he will not kill her.

steps.triggerLanguage: נֶעֶבְדָה בָּהּ עֲבֵירָה – אֵין מַצִּילִין אוֹתָהּ בְּנַפְשׁוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא, adding cases where the pursuer is not killed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The pursuer is not killed if the sin was already done, if she can be saved another way, or (according to רבי יהודה) if she says to leave him.

steps.title: Asking for the source of the ברייתא's list
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks where the ברייתא's cases come from.
steps.simpleTranslation: From where do we learn these things?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the Torah source of the cases in the ברייתא. This sets up the next step, where the source is given.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, sources were given only for murder and for a נערה המאורסה. Now the גמרא wants a source for the whole list in the new ברייתא, including a male and relationships punished by כרת or a court death penalty.

keyTerms.meaning: From where are these things learned?

phrases.english: From where are these matters derived?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of the list in the ברייתא.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The Torah source for killing a pursuer in each of the ברייתא's cases.

steps.title: One פסוק teaches all the cases
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא learns each case from a different word in דברים 22:26: נער, נערה, חטא, and מות.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says: 'And to the girl you shall do nothing; the girl has no sin worthy of death.' 'נער' teaches about a male. 'נערה' teaches about a נערה המאורסה. 'חטא' teaches about relationships punished by כרת. 'מות' teaches about relationships punished by a court death penalty.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question. It reads each word of one פסוק as pointing to a different case in the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the Torah the word is written נער, without the letter ה, but it is read נערה. The written form hints at a male, and the way it is read hints at the נערה המאורסה. The words חטא and מות add the כרת cases and the court death penalty cases.

keyTerms.meaning: The פסוק says
A young man; here it hints at a male victim
A sin; here it hints at כרת cases
Death; here it hints at court death penalty cases

steps.confusionAlert: נער and נערה are the same word in the פסוק. One reading comes from how it is written, and the other from how it is read.

phrases.english: The verse states:
"But to the young woman you shall do nothing;
the young woman has no sin worthy of death."
"Na'ar": this is a male,
phrases.notes: The word is written נער without a ה, so it can be read as a young man.

phrases.english: "Na'ara": this is a betrothed young woman,
"Sin": these are those liable to כרת,
"Death": these are those liable to a court death penalty.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר קְרָא: ״וְלַנַּעֲרָה לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה דָבָר אֵין לַנַּעֲרָה חֵטְא מָוֶת״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question by reading each word of one פסוק.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: דברים 22:26: נער teaches a male, נערה teaches a נערה המאורסה, חטא teaches כרת cases, and מות teaches court death penalty cases.
steps.whatToRemember: All the cases in the ברייתא come from one פסוק. Each of its four key words adds one case.

steps.title: Why does the פסוק need all these cases?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the Torah lists so many cases, if we could learn them from one another.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why do I need all of these?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the reading it just gave. If one case could teach the others, why would the פסוק need to hint at all four?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah does not waste words. If all four cases share the same rule, it seems that one example should be enough, so the extra cases need a reason. This sets up the explanation in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: Why do I need all of these?

phrases.english: Why do I need all these?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reading of the פסוק given in the previous step.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading that finds four separate cases in the פסוק.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the rule is the same in every case, one case should be enough to teach the rest. So the extra cases seem unnecessary.

steps.title: Each case is needed: the male case could not teach the נערה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that each case is needed. Had the Torah written only the male case, we would have thought the rule does not apply to a נערה.
steps.simpleTranslation: They are needed. If the Torah had written only 'נער', we would say the rule applies there because it is not a male's natural way. But a girl, for whom it is the natural way, we might say the rule does not apply.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins showing that each case is needed. It starts by explaining why we could not learn the נערה case from the male case. The next step explains the reverse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Forcing relations on a male is extra shameful and painful, because it is not the natural way. So we might have thought only that case is severe enough to allow killing the attacker. That is why the Torah must also teach the נערה case.

keyTerms.meaning: They are needed (each case teaches something new)
The Merciful One, meaning the Torah
His natural way
I might say no (the rule does not apply)

phrases.english: They are necessary,
for if the Merciful One had written only "na'ar,"
I would say that is because it is not his natural way,
but a young woman, for whom it is her natural way,
I might say no.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge by showing that each case is needed.
steps.terutzResolutionType: צריכותא: showing that each case teaches something the others could not
steps.terutzHavaAmina: With only נער written, we would think the rule applies just to a male, since it is not his natural way and is extra shameful.
steps.terutzMaskana: So the Torah also needed to write נערה, to teach that a נערה המאורסה is saved even at the cost of the attacker's life.

steps.title: Why the female case alone would not be enough
steps.stepSummary: Had the Torah written only נערה, we would think the rule applies only to her, because the attacker degrades her. A נער is not degraded in the same way, so we might think his attacker may not be killed.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if the Torah had written only 'נערה', we would say: she can be saved even by killing the attacker, because he degrades her. But a young man, who is not degraded that way, I would say no.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the other half of its answer. It shows that writing only the girl's case would also leave us with a wrong idea.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 21, the male case alone could not teach the female case. Now the reverse: the female case has a special reason, פגם (being degraded and losing her virginity), that the male case does not have. So we could not learn the נער from the נערה either, and both words are needed.

keyTerms.meaning: The Merciful One, meaning the Torah or ה׳
Degrades, causes a blemish or damage
A young man
I would say no, the rule would not apply

steps.whatToRemember: Each case has its own reason. The נערה is degraded, and the נער is not. So neither case can be learned from the other, and the Torah had to write both.

phrases.english: And if the Merciful One had written only "young woman"
phrases.notes: This is the word נערה in the פסוק (דברים 22:26), the betrothed girl who is being attacked.

phrases.english: [we would say it is] because he degrades her

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל נַעַר דְּלָא קָא פָגֵים לֵיהּ –
phrases.english: but a young man, whom he does not degrade
I would say no.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the two-sided answer begun in step 21, showing that the female case could not teach the male case either.
steps.terutzResolutionType: צריכותא: each case has its own reason, so neither can be learned from the other
steps.terutzHavaAmina: If only נערה were written, we would think killing the רודף is allowed only because she is degraded
steps.terutzMaskana: The Torah wrote נער too, so the rule applies even where there is no such degradation

steps.title: Setting up the next case: if the Torah had written both
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא starts the next part of its answer. It asks what we would think if the Torah had written only these two cases, נער and נערה.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if the Torah had written only these two cases...
steps.whatsHappening: This is a setup line. The גמרא is preparing to explain why even writing both the נער and the נערה would still not be enough.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא now accepts that both נער and נערה are needed. Next it will show that the other cases in the ברייתא (from the words חטא and מות) still add something these two cases could not teach. The end of this sentence comes on the next amud.

keyTerms.meaning: These, here meaning the two cases just discussed
And if, opening a 'what would we think' case

steps.confusionAlert: This sentence is not finished here. Don't look for the answer yet. The reason comes on the next amud.

phrases.english: And if the Merciful One had written [only] these
phrases.notes: 'These' means both cases just discussed, the young man and the young woman.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on step 22. Now that both נער and נערה are shown to be needed, it opens the question of why the other cases are needed too.
steps.terutzResolutionType: צריכותא continues: setting up why the further cases are needed
steps.terutzHavaAmina: If only נער and נערה were written, we might limit the rule to those kinds of cases (explained on the next amud)
